entries.content:
In “The Art of the Interview,” season four of the podcast The Critic and Her Publics, Merve Emre speaks with top writers and journalists to discuss the subtle skill of conducting an interview. The Review is collaborating with Lit Hub to publish transcripts and recordings of each episode.

I don’t understand why people talk to Isaac Chotiner. His reputation as the best interviewer-assassin at work today—maybe ever—precedes him. I suspect that each guest thinks he will be the one to finally best Chotiner. And he makes good use of this hubris. He calmly and respectfully dismantles the tendentious arguments people make about everything from the wars in Ukraine and the Middle East to gerrymandering, genocide denial, and deportation. But he also has an appreciation for deep knowledge. The opposite of the gotcha interview is the expert interview, when Chotiner lets people who know their trades inside out explain them to his devoted readership. As our conversation shows, the flip side of his savagery is his generosity.

Merve Emre: Are you used to being on the other end of this?

Isaac Chotiner: Yeah, but I’ll survive.

Can you tell us the story of how you got from being a college student to being the premier “assassin” interviewer?

I worked in politics briefly after graduating from college, on the John Kerry campaign in 2004. I wanted to give journalism a try and got a job at this thing called Bloggingheads.tv. It was ahead of its time, sort of a pre-podcast podcast where two writers or two academics would talk about political issues. Then I got an internship at Washington Monthly magazine, where I met a lot of people and got to do my first bits of writing. Next, I got an internship at The New Republic, where I worked as a fact-checker for a year and then stayed with the magazine for almost a decade. That was a really great experience for me. The position was called “Reporter Researcher” and was largely fact-checking, but you also got a chance to write, blog, meet writers, and go to the staff meetings. I stayed until 2014 when the whole staff basically quit because of a controversy about the new owner. I thought I was going to write a book, and then got dragged back into thinking I should cover Trump in some way in 2015–2016 and started doing it via interviewing. I worked at Slate and mostly did interviews there. Then I got hired by The New Yorker in 2019.

Why did you leave politics in the first place?

I probably would have gone into politics if Kerry had won. I was very interested in politics, and there were things I wanted to say, wanted to write, wanted to be expressive about in some way.

I was reading one of your early interviews in The New Republic this morning, which is your interview with V. S. Naipaul. You sent that to me as an example of an interview that you felt didn’t quite work out the way that you wanted it to. I was wondering if you could recreate the setting of that interview for us.

I’d started doing some interviews for The New Republic later in my time there, and then started interviewing authors. Naipaul has always been the writer that I’m most mesmerized by, despite his shortcomings, to be euphemistic, and so I got this interview with him in London. He was not a very friendly person, in the most basic way that someone is just not friendly. There are certain niceties that most people go through, and he just didn’t really do that. He had a very sweet, warm laugh, but was not a warm guy. And his wife, now widowed, Nadira Naipaul, was there too. I was very intimidated, partly because I have such awe for his work and partly because I hadn’t done many interviews, especially in person. And he just kind of browbeat me. He told me a lot of my questions were silly or would cut me off and so on.

But going back to that interview now, I think if I had a decade of experience interviewing, I would have been more aggressive, going back at him, and I think that may actually not have been the right way to do the interview. In some ways the interview works because his personality comes through, and so I always think of it as a reminder that sometimes you want to take a step back. Sometimes you need to take a step forward to pepper someone with questions or to correct something, but sometimes you also want to take a step back and get more of a sense of your interview subject that way.

One interesting thing happening in that interview is that Nadira never really goes away. She ends up becoming a kind of second subject of the interview, and I’m curious to hear you meditate on that. I found her continuous presence to be quite surprising.

Sometimes, for a variety of reasons, someone will want another person there with them during the interview, whether it’s a spouse or an agent or a PR-handler-type person. A lot of times interviewers say, “Oh no, it just has to be one-on-one. They can’t be in the room.” But my feeling is that if the other person wants to be there, fine, as long as everything they say is on the record too. And my hope is that it can help create an image of what the scene was like. I thought the dynamic between him and his wife was interesting. But she was very intimidating. We had more strange interactions after the formal interview was over, when they invited me to have lunch. There was a biography of Naipaul that had just come out, by Patrick French, an amazing authorized biography and very devastating in parts. Naipaul’s wife had this whole theory that the biography was mean because Patrick French had married an Indian, and since she was Pakistani, his wife had it out for her. All kinds of just crazy stuff. But she was a fascinating character. I also remember her saying that Jane Austen was ridiculous or something.

Yes, and that everybody agrees that Jane Austen is ridiculous, but you can’t get anybody to admit it because it’s such a taboo thing to say.

Exactly. Both had this thing of not just having very strong opinions but also claiming that anyone who thinks differently is just being politically correct.

Which is funny because he says in the interview that she’s there to keep him from saying anything too wicked. And then they’re both just saying extremely wicked things left and right.

With Naipaul, it was always, in part, a game. He was obviously a politically incorrect person, to use another euphemism, but I also think that saying the unsayable got to be part of his outward persona. In the Patrick French biography, there are all these letters that Naipaul had provided French, and they make Naipaul look horrible. French said that it was an act of great honesty, but also of great arrogance, to provide these letters, and that Naipaul has some sort of need to be seen as a monster in some sense.

Do you think he was trying to be monstrous with you? When I was reading the interview, it struck me that there were two rhetorical moves that he would use to be difficult. One was to barely answer a well-thought-out question of yours. Silence, essentially. And the second would be to turn the question on you to say, Where are you coming from? You have some kind of preconception about me, and all you want is for me to affirm your preconception. Both seem like two ways to, if not be monstrous, then at least refuse to play the game in the way a young interviewer would expect an older, more august person to play along.

In the moment, turning the questions back on me felt more manageable because you can at least talk, but the silence was definitely very tense. This is the same in human interactions, too—it doesn’t have to be an interview. If someone gives you the silent treatment, there’s kind of nothing worse. I don’t know that he was being monstrous in that sense, but I do think there is a desire to not play along with whatever the normal rules are perceived to be.

What would you have done differently, or what would you do now, if you felt like someone was refusing to play along with the rules that you were offering, or the rules that you wanted them to play by?

I probably would have made a meta comment on the way they were behaving. I would have said upfront, “You agreed to this interview. What’s the problem?” And that could be in the interview—we’re not going to cut that from the transcript. Those types of questions with an interview subject sometimes cause the other person to shut down, but sometimes they’re what gets them out of their shell.

You said earlier that silence is one of those things that’s difficult to manage in interviews as well as in ordinary human interactions. As we’ve been recording these episodes, it’s occurred to me how, for different people that we speak to, there are varying degrees of difference between an ordinary human interaction and an interview that is on the record for the purpose of publication. I’m curious to hear you think aloud about how the two feel different.

When I first started doing interviews, I felt anxious, not about the social interaction but about getting to all my questions, all the points I needed to make to draw out the other person, all the subjects I’d have to hit. In most interactions, you don’t think in that way. So that’s the most obvious difference. Additionally, what you’re mainly trying to do in a normal conversation is develop a rapport with the other person, or you already have a rapport and you’re trying to play off of it. And in an interview, you want that rapport, but you only want it to make sure their answers are more interesting, so they feel comfortable opening up. There’s something almost manipulative about it because you’re not actually trying to develop a rapport that’s going to last after the recorder gets turned off.

Advertisement

Has anyone ever been confused by that? Has anybody ever thought you were developing a rapport and felt betrayed?

Maybe some people who I’ve asked to do an interview with are surprised that it’s more hostile than they were expecting, but no, I don’t think so. It’s funny, I interviewed Hilary Mantel when I was at The New Republic, and spent a good chunk of the day with her. She was so nice and so warm that it was strange in that sense. We exchanged maybe ten or twelve emails over the next five years before she passed away, and she would always sign her emails “With love, Hilary.” It was this very sweet thing that I assume she did to almost everyone who wrote to her, but that was one moment where I felt like I genuinely liked this person, and it also made me sort of feel weird after the interview.

How do you think you developed the reputation as the “interview assassin” or the “gotcha” interviewer? How did we get to the point where McSweeney’s is writing parodies of you interviewing Santa Claus?

I guess I don’t mind being confrontational in interviews, so that became a type of interview I would occasionally do. But I’m not sure. I don’t want that to be the main type of interview that I do. But I’ve definitely learned that I have more of a tolerance for awkwardness on phone conversations than other people do.

As I was looking back through the interviews you’ve done for The New Yorker, I was thinking that there are two kinds you tend to do. You can tell me if this theory resonates with you. One is an interview where you want to expose some kind of illogic or hypocrisy that has real political and ethical stakes that a prominent person is touting. I’m thinking about your interviews with Howard Jacobson or Richard Epstein. They’re almost Socratic in the way you walk people through their own logic or through the things that they have written and try to get them to square circles that they can’t possibly square. And then the other type are these interviews where there are experts on particular subjects who you seem to feel like are owed a larger platform for their expertise to reach nonexpert audiences. It’s less about putting them through their paces and more about really letting them unfurl their knowledge through a set of questions that lets them make that knowledge palatable or accessible to the kinds of people who read The New Yorker.

That’s exactly right. To talk about the second type of interview, I always find that an interview with a smart person is way more interesting than reading an op-ed by that person. The way op-eds or short pieces work in newspapers or magazines is that often you’re making one specific point and arguing that point. And that’s fine, but there’s something about a conversation that lets you get a broader picture of an issue. I also think that you can do it without an argument. I’m definitely not opposed to making arguments, but hopefully a conversation about a subject can be more ruminative. Also, for me, there are so many subjects that I would not be comfortable writing about because I don’t feel like I know enough, but I do feel comfortable enough doing an interview. So interviews are a great way to be able to engage in all these different subjects that I’m fascinated by.

Well, that second kind of interview is also a reminder that there ought to be real expertise involved in making incredibly consequential foreign or domestic policy decisions. The op-ed is a really easy way to signal a political position, but it’s not a particularly good way to convey deep knowledge.

I feel that way too. One of the things I love about my job is getting to read in a variety of different subject areas, and then—I just started a book about Turkey—think, “Oh, could this author be someone that I talk to about Turkey a year from now?”

This isn’t a fair thing to say, but sometimes I almost feel like you’re doing the second kind of interview as penance for doing the first.

You know, I don’t feel so bad about doing the first type of interview. But I will say doing the more confrontational interviews is fun. If I haven’t done any in, say, six weeks, I think, “Oh, I should be doing something. There are so many people in public life who are so pathetic and awful and lying, and I should do an interview about that.” But then if I do two in three weeks, I’m just sort of like, “Oh God, can I please do an interview about something else.”

Let’s talk about how people get confrontational. One of the things that’s difficult with a transcript is that you have no sense of people’s tone, either your tone or the interviewee’s tone. Do you feel like you ask questions in a hostile way? How would you describe your tone?

I would say that my way of doing this has changed as the era that we’re in has progressed. There are some people who are really serious and I think may have compromised themselves intellectually in some way, or have certain hypocrisies, or are just mistaken on an issue of great importance. I think it would be interesting to poke at their arguments to make a conversation. In those interviews I sometimes ask questions that are very direct, and you can tell where I’m coming from. But I don’t think they are perceived as hostile. There are other people in public life with whom I don’t think that type of confrontational interview means anything anymore. The idea of pointing out intellectual hypocrisy in Trump administration officials doesn’t interest me. But what does interest me is the insanity of the world we’re living in, so I would hope that interviews I do on that score try to be kind of funny or ridiculous in a way that shines a spotlight on this era.

In some ways, what ends up being ridiculous are the people’s own reactions to your questions. Richard Epstein melting down over you simply reading things that he has written back to him or Howard Jacobson becoming highly emotional and ranting all over the place aren’t about exposing the failures of arguments so much as failures of temperament and character.

I would just say that for Jacobson, that’s kind of how he is these days. The Epstein one was a very abnormal interview in terms of how he was on the phone. Most interviews are very polite. There have been only a few interviews where the person seemed really upset or angry. Epstein was one of them. Although he seemed okay by the end, he kind of lost his cool in the middle of the interview. You actually don’t want someone to get too upset because the main thing you want is for them to be thoughtful in answering the questions, and when any of us get upset, that’s not what we are. So I try to keep the temperature pretty low. But there’s also just a polite way to ask direct questions, and that’s what I try to do in most cases.

I feel like it’s actually incredibly difficult to ask a direct question calmly and politely. People find all sorts of ways to hedge, to walk things back.

Honestly, I think the fact that I get to do so many of these interviews on the phone is the reason that it’s easier. I don’t think I could do it in person.

Why?

For the reasons you say—it’s hard to look someone in the eye and ask them awkward questions. On the phone, it’s much easier. God bless the phone in that sense. There are some interviews that you really want to do in person, to see and to understand the person. But for other interviews, it’s great to be on the phone.

Why do you think people still say yes to interviews with you when they know or suspect that they’re going to be in that first category of interview subject?

Well, you and I are both writers, and we read bylines. Most people don’t read bylines or have a great sense of who they’re talking to and what the person wants. I also think people just like to talk. I always think back to this piece Michael Lewis wrote for The New York Times Magazine in 2003 about the California recall election where you had all these crazy people who were running. The sense of the piece is that so many people just want to talk and have their voices heard and feel understood. Plus, most of the time, people think that they come across well in interviews. I don’t mean to say that they don’t, but most people think what they say is interesting and smart. I have a couple people in my life who have very different political views than I do. One is an old family friend who is much more conservative than I am and sometimes writes to me about my interviews, and he has a completely different take on them. I always think it’s so interesting to have his perspective because it’s a reminder that you can think an interview reads one way, and someone else can read it in a totally different way.

When have you been most surprised by how an interview was received?

I would say I’m always shocked when reading transcripts by how differently they come across compared to how the conversation went. Sometimes it’s very similar and sometimes you’re like, “I didn’t hear the person the way they meant this,” or “This actually connects back to this, and I didn’t realize it.” And that’s a fascinating thing for me. And—I’ve talked about this with my editors before—sometimes a completely faithful editing of a conversation, i.e., no editing, can leave a misleading impression of what was happening.

Can you be more specific about occasions when not editing an interview transcript feels like it’s doing a disservice to the conversation itself?

Sometimes people will say “Well” and “Um” and “Hmm” and it’ll make it seem like they’re planning to say something that’s not true or coming up with an excuse. But when you’re listening to the conversation, you know that they are in fact just thinking out loud. So if you include their hemming and hawing, then you make them seem less prepared and less insightful than they are. Other times, people will pause and hem and haw, and it’s clearly a sign that they realized they’ve said something they shouldn’t have, and they’re figuring out how to back out of it. Sometimes you can tell by someone’s tone that they thought a joke or comment you just made was funny, but they will not laugh, and sometimes they will laugh in a way that is clearly meant to be polite, but they did not think the joke you just told was funny. Those sorts of nuances get lost frequently in very literal transcripts, so it’s interesting to think through how to edit that stuff.

What about writing the introduction? I was struck by the difference between the intro to, say, the Naipaul piece and subsequent headers. That really does emphasize his bad behavior in his first marriage, and sets us up to receive him in a particular way. The introductions you write for The New Yorker interviews are much more neutral, or they read much more neutrally to me, even when they are with someone who I assume you’re about to show as being objectionable or insane or hysterical.

The Naipaul one was my favorite I ever got to write because he told me this crazy story about his cat at lunch, and I knew I couldn’t have it in the Q and A portion so needed to get it in the intro. Sometimes I’m interviewing someone and the reader doesn’t care that much about who I’m interviewing, they’re just interested in the subject matter. For example, when interviewing someone about an election in India, it’s not like the political scientist I choose at some Indian college is of huge interest to most readers. Whereas if I’m interviewing V. S. Naipaul or Zadie Smith, people want to know a lot about V. S. Naipaul or Zadie Smith. So I try and have more in-depth intros to give some flavor of the conversation. If the interview is kind of ridiculous, I try to be tongue-in-cheek in the intro. But other times, I’m just thinking that people do not want to read a long intro; they just want to get to the Q and A.

There is a parody of your interviews in Current Affairs where you’re interviewing Henry VIII, and the first question is, “Did you kill Anne Boleyn?” and he’s like, “Well, no, the executioner did.” There is this way people will sometimes try to weasel their way out of your questions by being like, “Well, you think the cause of X was Y, but actually the cause of X was this much more proximate thing.” I love those kinds of questions. They build a whole political system in the asking and the answering.

It’s funny you say that. I’ve often thought that what people assign cause and effect to, and what they don’t, is one of the most telling things about how they think. Some people think that NATO expansion caused Putin to invade Russia, and some people think that Israeli policies in Gaza caused Hamas to kill people on October 7, and some people think that Hamas killing people on October 7 caused Israel to flatten Gaza. And without making a judgment on any of these things, I think the way in which people use the language of “this caused this” often gets to their fundamental values, because in other cases you don’t use the language of cause and effect. You sort of explain things as just being. To give an obvious example, lots of people grow up with really terrible fathers. Some of them are the Trump kids, but nobody excuses their behavior by saying, “Well, they did grow up with the worst father on earth,” because a lot of people don’t have sympathy for the Trump kids. And so, in our daily language, the way we talk about cause and effect is really telling.

One way that I think of you at the magazine is as the person who does most of the Q and As, but the other way that I think about you is the person who’s been at the forefront of the The New Yorker’s coverage and its moral position on the genocide in Gaza since October 7. I’m wondering if you feel that way too.

I know there have been a lot of complaints about the media coverage of Gaza, some of which I agree with, but broadly speaking, I’m happy with what the magazine has done with it, and I’m glad that the editors there have encouraged me to keep doing Gaza coverage. For me, the story is important not simply because of what’s going on in Gaza but also because of the conversation here about it. I thought it was important for The New Yorker readers to look into.

What do you mean by the conversation here about it?

I’m not totally naive about who reads The New Yorker, and if I’m doing an interview about people being sent to a gulag in El Salvador by the Trump administration, I’m pretty confident that 99 percent of the readers at The New Yorker feel the same way about it that I do. But in a lot of the period before January 2025, what was going on in Gaza and the debate in the Democratic Party and the Biden administration was something people on the left had very different opinions on from each other. It felt like the stated commitments of a Democratic administration—especially because this was going on at the same time as the war in Ukraine, about which the Biden administration was making broad claims about the importance of democracy and human rights—were being tested in the Middle East. There were a lot of different avenues for Q and As among all these related topics, as well as just the humanitarian situation on the ground in Gaza.

I’ve been an admirer of those interviews. I’ve been wondering if you want them to change opinions among center-left readers of The New Yorker. Is there a kind of conversion project there?

No, I don’t think of it in those terms at all. Rather, hypocrisy is really interesting to me. It’s not that I think hypocrisy is the greatest sin, because I think we’re all hypocrites—I actually don’t even think it’s really a sin—but I do think it exposes other things. When you start to understand why you’re hypocritical, you understand your own double standards and your way of looking at the world, or how you were raised to see things in a certain way. And so I thought the hypocrisy shown by the Biden administration with regard to Israel was a really interesting way of getting at all these other issues.

What are your most abiding hypocrisies?

Oh, that’s a good question. I need someone else to point that out to me because, you know, we often can’t point out our own hypocrisies. Then we would just change them or try to change them.

I suppose that’s true. I should have come better prepared to interview you the way you would have interviewed someone.

I wish someone would point out my hypocrisies. You get a lot of letters when you do interviews and some of them are completely insane, but sometimes someone will point out, like, “You said this in this interview and you know three months ago you made this point about this separate subject and how do these mesh,” and you’ll be like, “I should have thought harder about that.” It doesn’t mean I’m a bad person or something—again, I don’t view hypocrisy as a sin—but it definitely makes me think, “Why does that dissonance exist?”

I wonder if that dissonance exists because you shift your own political or moral positions in order to have more hostile or more tense and interestingly combative encounters with different people you’re interviewing. I wonder if you really are itching for a fight.

Maybe I’m being naive here, but I don’t think I’m itching for a fight. I definitely get angry about things I read in the news and think, “Oh, I should do an interview about this.” I feel like I’m kind of immune to feeling awkward about a fight, but I don’t feel like I’m itching for it. But again, maybe someone can correct me and tell me that this is wrong. It’s very possibly wrong.

entries.title: Qusra Under Siege
entries.summary: Another Palestinian village in the West Bank has been attacked by Israeli settlers. The lack of response by the army and police reveals how deeply corrupted they are by the colonialist agenda.
entries.source: The New York Review of Books
entries.content:
If you’d like to know who is sovereign in the State of Israel today, consider the fate of the village of Qusra in the central West Bank, close to Nablus. On August 9 dozens of crazed Israeli settlers began a siege of three Palestinian houses at the edge of the village, homes to the families of Yusuf Hasan, Riziq Hasan, and Qusay Abu Riddy. The settlers blocked all access roads and paths, invaded the courtyards of the houses, stoned doors and windows, cut the electricity lines and the water pipes, and prevented any supplies from entering. Inside the houses, food reserves were dwindling fast and there was very little water. Temperatures in August are over one hundred degrees Fahrenheit in Qusra. The death of the family members by thirst and starvation was definitely a possibility. One of the children was in acute need of medical care, but the settlers delayed the Palestinian ambulance coming to take her to the hospital.

All this is routine in the Palestinian West Bank. Equally routine is the response of the Israeli army and police. Soldiers arrived on August 10, fraternized with the settlers, prayed with them, and declared the area a Closed Military Zone. In theory a CMZ is supposed to exclude anyone who is not actually a resident, but the rules of CMZs never apply to settlers. They did apply to the Israeli activists who were trying to get through to the besieged families with food and water; first the settlers, then the soldiers, or both together, turned them back.

Qusra has suffered from constant settler pogroms over the last few months. On July 26 settlers burned down the al-Rahma mosque in the village. Around that time armed settlers brutally attacked Palestinian farmers from the village and the Israeli and international activists who were trying to protect them; several were severely wounded. In March twenty-eight-year-old Amir Moatasem Odeh was killed by a settler; another stabbed his father.1 A few weeks earlier, on February 27, settlers stormed into Qusra and nearly clubbed to death two activists who are friends of mine; a third activist managed to film the attack. The settler assassins were arrested by the police and as usual released within a few hours. No action has been taken against them. Settlers are above and beyond the law.

This time the Qusra siege quickly made its way into the Israeli and the international press, and there was outrage and a demand for action. The commanding general of the West Bank, Avi Bluth, was compelled to visit the village to see what was happening there (as if he didn’t know). He issued a strong statement calling the invading settlers criminals and has recently even spoken of them as inflicting “Jewish terror.” His record on Palestinian matters on the whole is, however, abysmal. He has proudly said that the army is now “killing like we haven’t killed since 1967.” The IDF chief of staff, Eyal Zamir, announced that a battalion of reserve soldiers was being diverted from training exercises to Qusra. The soldiers came, stayed an hour or two, and left. The siege continued unabated.

However, the soldiers did remove a makeshift sunshade that the settlers had put up. The redoubtable Israeli army, supposedly capable of fighting off enemies in Iran, Syria, Lebanon, and Yemen all at once, has now added to its glory the removal of a ragtag canopy in a daring commando raid. The chief of staff must have thought the battle had been won.

On the fifth day of the siege, the army returned to the village and destroyed the outpost that the settlers had put in place as well as two other settler outposts in the immediate vicinity. The siege of the houses was briefly breached. Within hours the settlers had created a new outpost in the wadi some two hundred to three hundred meters away from those houses. It is likely to remain in place indefinitely, unless a minimally rational government wins the elections in October. There are now close to two hundred such outposts all over the West Bank, including in Areas A and B—the former supposedly under full Palestinian control, the latter under Palestinian civil jurisdiction and Israeli security authority. Qusra is in Area B. You can see how much authority the army chooses to exercise in Area B; it is even more subservient to the settlers in Area C, under total Israeli control. Here lies the answer to the question of sovereignty I posed at the outset.

The settlers’ siege tactic has worked well in other villages, including Jalud, very close to Qusra, where a home belonging to the Tubasi family was “conquered” and the family driven out. We experienced much the same thing firsthand last winter in Ras al-’Ain, in the Jordan Valley, where a new settler outpost situated inside the village succeeded in expelling all 1,200 of the Bedouin shepherds who lived there.2 We are now, as I write, facing a similar situation at the village of At-Tawa’il, on the ridge overlooking the Jordan Valley. Along with the cancerous outpost, there are episodic attacks on the Palestinian shepherds and their houses. Just over a month ago, a masked settler invaded the home of ‘Imad and his wife, Amal, after midnight and tried to beat them to death; fortunately two of our activists were close by, heard the screams, and managed to drive the settler away.

Advertisement

One might expect that the soldiers who are now in Qusra would arrest at least a few of the instigators of the siege. Dozens of settler thugs are still freely roaming the village. One was apparently detained for a few minutes and then released. There have been no arrests, and none are to be expected. To make some kind of sense of all this, one has to understand how deeply corruption has spread in the army and the police. The rank and file have sold their souls to Itamar Ben-Gvir, the Kahanist convicted criminal whom Benjamin Netanyahu appointed minister of national security. Occasionally we hear indirectly from high-ranking officers on the West Bank that they are helpless in the face of political pressure from the extreme right. It would be closer to the truth to say that these officers, too, are party to the brutal attacks. In any case, the orders come from the settlers, though just behind them sits the nefarious prime minister, intent on destruction, and the mindless ministers of his government.

We are hoping for honest elections on October 27. So far nearly all the polls show that a large majority of Israelis—close to two thirds—want to rid themselves of Netanyahu and the extreme right. Even among members of the Likud party, Netanyahu’s base, there has been alienation and unrest, almost reaching the level of a putsch. Even they can see that he has failed at everything he has touched, including the two Iran wars. But we are more than a little worried that he will concoct some emergency in order to cancel or postpone the elections; he and his sycophants will very likely try to rig them one way or another if they do take place. Some optimistic people say that if Netanyahu steals the election, the mass antigovernment demonstrations that took place before the Gaza war will revive, with millions in the streets. However, two and a half months is almost an eternity in Israel; much can happen before the end of October.

There remains the question of how Israel has sunk so low, how it has desecrated the foundational ethos of the state and the values it once held dear. I have at times tried, in these pages, to offer some preliminary explanations. One thing is certain: the occupation and the settler enterprise constitute the deep, recalcitrant core of all our troubles.

Earlier this year the historian Omer Bartov published a book on this topic, Israel: What Went Wrong?3 (The answer is: everything.) It’s easy, and in fact correct, to blame a majority of the religious Zionists for legitimizing the settler colonial project on the West Bank, with its appalling messianic-apocalyptic ideology. (A humane exception is the group Bnei Avraham—young religious Zionists, many of them born and raised in the settlements, who have chosen to actively protect Palestinians from the sadistic settlers.) I’m told by an acquaintance in one of the long-established “mainstream” settler towns in the territories that the settlers there are divided fifty-fifty: half are disgusted by the rampaging violence, and the other half are in favor of it. She used to be hesitantly horrified by settler violence; now she supports it.

By now there are well over half a million Jewish settlers on the West Bank (worth ten to twelve seats in the Knesset). The vicious outpost settlers are a small minority—many hundreds, perhaps a thousand or more, no one knows for sure—but they, in more ways than one, enact the colonialist agenda. From my vantage point, after long experience in the field, it seems that thuggery, including murder, is profoundly pleasurable—a crude semisexual delight—for the perpetrators. Once it’s been rationalized and authorized by the government, even admired and cultivated as an expedient virtue, there’s no easy way to stop it.

I know these settlers all too well. Some of them are derelict minors who have been captured by the settler organizations, taken to outposts in the Palestinian territories, brainwashed, and taught to kill. The older ones are fully committed to the ethnic cleansing of the West Bank and to the cherished hope that a full-scale war there will enable them to expel two and a half million Palestinians. That won’t happen. What may well happen, if the opposition fails to win the election, is annexation of the territories, along with maybe a few chunks of Lebanon and even Syria for good measure, and a brittle but lethal apartheid regime. Once we pointed out to the settler sheriff Noam Jackson, whom we meet most days in At-Tawa’il, that this lovely village he covets sits on privately owned Palestinian land. He shifted the gun he carries around his shoulder and said, “There is no such thing as Palestinian land.”

Advertisement

As for Qusra, the siege is now in its third week. The families are barricaded in their homes. They know that if they succumb to the settlers’ threats and leave, their houses will be lost forever. Despite the international uproar, the outlook is very bleak. Like some eighty other Palestinian villages on the West Bank, Qusra may fall. Still, on August 14, a convoy of a hundred or so Israeli and Palestinian peace activists got through the army barriers and delivered food and water to the families. Sometimes good things happen, with a little courage.

—August 26, 2026

entries.content:
On a muggy morning in late July, when tens of thousands of protesters thronged to central New Delhi to head toward parliament, they seemed to already have a sense that their march might be historic. Most were students and young graduates, many of whom had traveled from towns hundreds of miles away to attend their very first protest. As I squeezed through the crowd I saw posters with cartoons of a bespectacled, mustached man accompanied by varied fonts spelling the word RESIGN—a reference to the rally’s central demand that India’s education minister, Dharmendra Pradhan, step down after presiding over a disastrous exam-paper leak. But nearly as common were portraits of revolutionaries from the Indian independence struggle: M.K. Gandhi, the Dalit leader B.R. Ambedkar, and, most ubiquitous that day, Bhagat Singh.

Born in 1907 in Banga (in present-day Pakistan), Singh became an anticolonial militant in 1928, when the seven-member Indian Statutory Commission—popularly known as the “Simon Commission” after its chief, John Simon—arrived in India to assess conditions for constitutional reforms. As it moved from city to city across the colony, the commission, which had no Indian members, was met with swarms of protesters chanting “Simon go back.” At a demonstration in Lahore led by the Indian nationalist Lala Lajpat Rai, the police brutally beat protesters; Rai soon died of his injuries.

Singh and his associates, seeking to avenge Rai’s death, plotted to assassinate the superintendent who had authorized the police violence, but they ended up killing the wrong man. Singh evaded arrest until four months later, in April 1929, when he and a comrade threw small, non-lethal bombs inside Delhi’s Central Legislative Assembly, hoping to incite a “proletariat revolution.” Rather than turn fugitive again, Singh stayed on the scene, shouting revolutionary slogans and then submitting to arrest. In the widely publicized trial that followed, he used the courtroom to spread an anticolonial message, especially to the country’s youth. In prison he went on hunger strike, calling for better treatment for Indian political prisoners. Until his death he maintained that his acts of violence weren’t “aimless outrages” but calculated political moves toward freedom. “Let me announce with all the strength at my command, that I am not a terrorist,” he wrote from Lahore Central Jail in 1931, less than two months before he was hanged.

On a banner pegged to a metal fence beside the road that morning in Delhi, Singh appeared in an oval frame flanked by his comrades Rajguru and Sukhdev, who were executed with him. Nearby, a man pressed through the crowd wearing a white t-shirt adorned with black-marker lettering: “GLORY TO BHAGAT SINGH.” Many of the marchers’ signs and posters bore a particular studio portrait of Singh in a felt hat tilted to the left. In it his face is clean-shaven except for a wiry mustache that barely obscures his otherwise boyish appearance. Emblazoned in Hindi beneath one replica of the image that day—on a poster produced by a left-wing student group—was the phrase “Looks like I gotta come back, bro.”

Although the nonviolent student protesters had markedly different methods than Singh’s, he nonetheless seemed to symbolize something central to their struggle. In a sense this was hardly surprising. Nearly eighty years after India gained independence, the rhetoric of national integrity still dominates public life, even in everyday chatter. Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s Hindu-nationalist Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP), which has governed the country since 2014, claims to be restoring the land to precolonial glory, while its critics call to safeguard the nation’s “true” inclusive values against such divisive forces. It isn’t uncommon for Indian protests to invoke historical figures in this spirit. In recent years Gandhi and Ambedkar have emerged as a diptych embodying the secular constitutional principles on which the Indian republic was founded, while Singh—long an emblem of radical left-wing student politics—has been idealized, even coopted, by groups across the political spectrum. The mythology of this young man feverishly dedicated to his country has been immortalized in several Bollywood films, with rousing dialogue about how “freedom” was his “bride” and violent scenes of him being force-fed by the British while on hunger strike.

But his renewed prominence at this protest still felt significant. Those signs and posters at once suggested the growing influence of left-wing student activism in this moment and pointed to a more expansive sensibility among the crowd. By turning to a student leader from the colonial past, the many nonaffiliated protesters, too, seemed to argue that they were fighting to reform not just a few untenable policies but the nation itself. Over the four weeks that the protests gathered strength, this broad-brush anticolonial rhetoric came to have complicated implications. It allowed thousands of people with discrepant political leanings to position themselves as a righteous collective and contest Modi’s monopoly on the language of national preservation; it also downplayed the real political divisions among the protesters and the concerns of the communities, especially Muslims, who have borne the brunt of public dissent in recent years.

Advertisement

The protesters frequently invoked the past, but their movement’s direct triggers were squarely in the present. In May of this year a group of experts hired by the National Testing Agency allegedly leaked the questions for the government’s centralized medical entrance exam after 2.27 million candidates had taken the test. This was hardly the first time in recent memory that a major public exam’s results had been invalidated because of administrative negligence. Over the last five years at least forty-five major exams have been similarly leaked. In a country with a harrowingly competitive education system and an increasingly bleak job market (nearly 40 percent of graduates under twenty-five are unemployed), such leaks are reported to have driven dozens of students to suicide over the last decade.

Only three days after this latest leak, the chief justice of the Indian Supreme Court unwittingly exacerbated the situation when he made a comment likening unemployed youth to “cockroaches.” As the online response escalated, Abhijeet Dipke, a Boston University graduate based in the US, joked on social media: “What if all cockroaches come together?” The proposition quickly gathered earnest supporters, who rallied under the banner of the “Cockroach Janata Party” (CJP). Calling themselves the “voice of the lazy and unemployed,” they soon steered their efforts toward a mass youth campaign for educational reform. In a broken public education system, they declared, accountability would begin only once Pradhan resigned.

It wasn’t a small demand. Dozens of crises had come and gone during Modi’s twelve years in power, from the overnight demonetization of high-value currency to widespread mismanagement of the Covid-19 pandemic, without a single cabinet minister stepping down. Pradhan was a crucial member both of the BJP and of Modi’s inner circle, having secured the party’s victory in the state of Odisha. To call for his resignation was to challenge the highest rung of a famously unyielding government.

The CJP is in numerous respects a regulated organization: it has a declared leadership, official spokespeople, and now even a working committee. From its earliest days, however, it adamantly professed that it wasn’t a political or ideological party, and soon it had the support of groups with competing visions for the movement. Left-wing organizations like the All India Students Association (AISA) and the Students Federation of India (SFI)—both affiliated with Indian communist parties—had rallied against the government’s educational policies for several years, and both of them backed the CJP’s demands. Seasoned at protesting across Delhi’s college campuses and streets, these groups attracted swaths of student supporters; they also formed organized blocs within an otherwise largely spontaneous show of dissent.

In the third week of June a motley constellation of protesters started camping out at Jantar Mantar, a backstreet in central Delhi authorized by police as the city’s venue for demonstrations. When it became clear that the government had little intention of engaging with the agitators’ demands, the prominent Ladakhi education and environmental activist Sonam Wangchuk went on hunger strike in support of the cause. Three students from AISA joined him, invoking their hero Bhagat Singh. Although AISA and Wangchuk disagreed on several crucial points (Wangchuk supported the controversial National Education Policy implemented by the government in 2020, while AISA called for it to be scrapped entirely), they continued to fast alongside each other for the next three weeks.

The CJP leaders and Wangchuk sat on an imposing stage at one end of the meagre site, while students set up smaller tents on either side. Throughout the day they beat a drum, chanting slogans—“Long live the revolution!” “Dharmendra Pradhan, resign, resign!”—while their fasting comrades lay on low platforms behind them. Soon images started traveling across social media of the fifty-nine-year-old educator and the self-sacrificing students being propped up by aides just to get to the bathroom. Sympathizers flocked to Jantar Mantar in larger and larger numbers. Then, on July 18, Delhi police intruded on the scene. They bundled away Wangchuk behind a cordon of white bedsheets, claiming they were under court orders to hospitalize him.

Videos of the operation burned through social media. If the government hoped that removing Wangchuk would quell the protests, it had just the opposite effect: overnight he became a symbol of the Modi government’s apathy toward the country’s education crisis. Two days later, on July 20, the streets around Jantar Mantar were bursting, far beyond anyone’s expectations, with protesters ready to march to parliament. By then I had resolved to show up at Jantar Mantar every day, hoping to observe the movement from up close.

Advertisement

That morning the police had deemed the rally an unlawful assembly, and signboards on the road leading to Jantar Mantar warned people they were breaking the law just by attending. Five metro stations in the vicinity had been sealed and mobile Internet services suspended, so that people in one section of the protest had no sense of what was happening in another. Barricaded by police and paramilitary forces into a tiny area (less than a kilometer at its widest), the crowd jostled for an exit route. I pushed my way through from Parliament Street back to the Janpath metro station, and then toward the Press Club on Raisina Road.

As the demonstration swelled outward from Jantar Mantar, police and paramilitary troops from the Rapid Action Force—few of whom seemed to be wearing their standard identifying badges—shot several rounds of tear gas into the crowd. The people around me ran in panic, some almost trampling each other. When I met up with colleagues a safe distance away, one of them told me the police had cleared the stage and pulled down the tents that had sheltered the camping strikers at the protest’s center. A few streets away, a friend reported, police had beaten unarmed marchers with batons, leaving a number of people with fractured limbs and bleeding heads. Later, as I walked along the emptied streets, I saw scattered protesters hobbling with bruises on their legs. Shoes and slippers lay strewn on the road. In a couple of hours videos would make the rounds online of masked men in plainclothes beating protesters alongside the uniformed officers; the police haven’t clarified who they were.

Eyewitnesses uploaded videos over the next twenty-four hours, and it emerged that paramilitary officers had fired into the crowd with “pellet” shotguns at another spot in central Delhi. Until now such guns, which lodge small metal pellets beneath the skin of anyone in the line of fire, had been a trademark of Indian security forces’ tactics in Kashmir, where the weapons have injured thousands of civilians, blinded more than a hundred, and killed more than a dozen since they were introduced for crowd control in 2010. The firing around Jantar Mantar was the first known instance of law enforcement using them in the national capital. Indian and international media would soon confirm that a number of protesters were treated for pellet injuries at local hospitals; at least two had been hit with multiple pellets in the face and neck.

But these violent tactics, too, soon backfired: by evening, enraged by the brutal treatment of their classmates and peers, hundreds of protesters had reclaimed the demolished encampment and the areas surrounding it. By the next day the crowd seemed to have multiplied fourfold. As videos of the attacks spread through social media, supporters swarmed to Jantar Mantar from across the country. Some brought food and water; others volunteered as garbage cleaners. Within two days the crowd had grown into a sticky mass of bodies with barely any space between them. Meanwhile, dozens of satellite protests of varying sizes formed in cities and towns hundreds of miles from the capital. At Jantar Mantar I met a shoe factory worker from Agra, a bike mechanic from Meerut, and an accountant who had a stable job in Delhi, all of whom had turned out in support of the students after seeing the scenes of violence. They had come, as the mechanic told me, for “India’s future.”

Each of the disparate groups converging on Jantar Mantar brought their own grievances. Some were frustrated they hadn’t been able to find work for years, despite the government’s promises that the job market would improve. Others were sick of seeing the Modi administration double down on religious propaganda but neglect issues like education, health care, and the toll of inflation. Still others wanted to draw attention to environmental crises abetted by the government and its billionaire allies. Many were veterans of anti-caste organizing (Dipke is himself Dalit and a professed Ambedkarite), while others were, as several admitted to me, longtime BJP supporters. What started as a protest about education was now a mélange of every possible complaint against Modi’s regime.

Previous surges of demonstrations against the BJP—including the protests against the flagrantly anti-Muslim Citizenship (Amendment) Act in 2019–2020 and the farmers’ protests in 2020—had been led by marginalized groups. The state singled out these communities, and especially Muslims, for violent repression in response; there were no large protests against this targeted crackdown. Memories of those episodes were still fresh when the recent youth protests got underway, and many Muslim students felt wary about further risking their safety to join a movement that made little explicit reference to Muslim persecution. But after the police started brutalizing dominant-caste Hindus, too, something began to shift. Finding themselves under direct fire for the first time, the majority grew bolder about standing up to the state. Some protesters, however cautiously, even started criticizing the government’s anti-Muslim actions.

This shift was most apparent in the way the protesters changed their target after the bloodbath on July 20. Now, more than Pradhan, most of the agitators seemed to direct their anger at Modi himself. I heard several groups demand the prime minister’s resignation, with some shouting “Whenever Modi is scared, he pits Hindus against Muslims.” “FUCK MODI” graffiti spread around the area; rhyming chants called the prime minister a coward, a monkey, and a pimp. With increasing frequency, people also brought AI-generated, often misogynistic caricatures that depicted Modi as a voluptuous prostitute “asking for it” or as a servile tradwife groveling before Donald Trump.

But the protesters’ disaffection was hardly unified. Walking through the crowd after July 20, it wasn’t difficult to see the faultlines. When anti-caste groups waving blue flags shouted “Jai Bhim” in praise of Ambedkar, young people who admitted having until recently had Hindu-nationalist sympathies shouted in unison with them. The odd person even attempted to add “Jai Shri Ram”—a hallmark of anti-Muslim rhetoric—to the chorus. At one point CJP leaders, evidently hoping to keep up the pretense that their movement wasn’t “political,” tried to stop protesters from initiating a popular call-and-response sequence calling for azadi (“freedom”) that has been associated with demands for Kashmiri independence, a view considered seditious under Indian law. Students from left-wing groups chanted with gusto all the same.

In one sense the campaign owed its energy and its numbers precisely to its non-ideological posture. This was a generation of protesters that had only ever known life under the BJP, and to many of them rejecting that politics seemed to require rejecting political commitments wholesale. By claiming to focus on nondenominational issues like exam leaks, many of the demonstrators were also, in effect, arguing that they didn’t deserve the state’s retaliation.

None of this prevented the movement from adopting a more audacious style than any other in recent years. In a culture that hammers on about respecting one’s elders and figures of authority, these young protesters chose to make profanity their lingua franca. Several flaunted sexualized posters: “Daddy, beat me,” “Arrest me but make it sexy,” “My life is so blessed that I got to fuck Dharmendra Pradhan in the ass.” The effect of this new tone is hard to overstate: it did profound damage to Modi’s stoic, sage-like image, which until now he had used to cast himself as a father figure for the nation.

But after the mass violence a more focused political critique also started to emerge around Jantar Mantar. Recalling the Simon Commission’s unceremonious welcome, fresh graffiti on barricades read “MODI GO BACK” and “SIMON COME BACK.” On a wall close by, another slogan in Hindi invoked the British official who, in 1919, ordered the army to open fire onto a crowd of unarmed civilians at Jallianwala Bagh in Amritsar: “OUR PRIME MINISTER IS A COWARD. HE’S ANOTHER GENERAL DYER.” At a press conference Delhi’s former chief minister, Arvind Kejriwal, of the Aam Aadmi Party, echoed the sentiment: “What General Dyer did at Jallianwala Bagh has been surpassed by Modi.”

If the protesters wanted to gain the sympathies of Indians across the country, they knew, they had to appeal to a universal sense of patriotism. Over the years the BJP has used film, pop music, and straight-up oratory propaganda to bolster its reputation as India’s historic defender. Just last November Modi declared that his government would free the country from its degenerate “colonial mindset” by reviving the region’s Hindu past. By likening Modi’s administration to colonizers, a demographically broad set of people at Jantar Mantar were, with striking success, taking this mythos apart.

The BJP rebuked the protesters using all the expected slurs, from “anti-national” to “terrorists.” There was a certain irony here—for the BJP’s own origins lie in another mass student movement with far more militant tactics. In the 1970s campus protests in the states of Gujarat and Bihar snowballed into a comprehensive agitation against government corruption. The students, who blockaded roads and torched government buildings, eventually called for the resignation of Indira Gandhi, who was then the prime minister. Although led by a generally nonpartisan activist named Jayaprakash Narayan, the students were supported by an unlikely coalition of Indira’s opponents—including members of the Jana Sangh, which would go on to become the BJP. An important share of the movement’s organizational direction, too, had come from the Akhil Bharatiya Vidyarthi Parishad (ABVP), the student wing of the Hindu-supremacist Rashtriya Swayamsevak Sangh (RSS), which is the ideological parent organization of the BJP.

Over Modi’s three terms in office, the BJP government has literally rewritten history textbooks, glorifying Hindu figures and vilifying Muslim ones. In the same revisionist spirit, the party seems to have worked to expunge the memory of the student activism that was so crucial to its own rise. Now that another brand of students is confronting Modi’s government not unlike how the BJP’s forebears did Indira’s, history seems to be repeating itself—much to the ruling party’s inconvenience.

Today, any youth movement that wants to seriously contest Modi’s claim on India’s past and future will have to contend directly with the Hindu-nationalist dimensions of the BJP’s repression. At Jantar Mantar, a number of factions—especially the left-wing student groups—repeatedly called attention to the government’s manipulation of caste and religion, often drawing on ideas developed by earlier iterations of the student movement under BJP rule.

Back in 2016, when Modi had barely been in office for two years, student protests erupted across the country, with caste at their center. Their immediate catalyst was the news that Rohith Vemula, a Ph.D. student at the University of Hyderabad in southern India who identified as Dalit, had died by suicide after university authorities revoked his on-campus housing, accusing him and four other members of the Ambedkar Students Association of roughing up an ABVP student leader. Vemula strongly denied the allegation, arguing that he was being targeted because of his caste and his participation in anti-caste Ambedkarite organizing. “The value of a man was reduced to his immediate identity,” he wrote in his suicide note, referring to his Dalit background. “My birth is my fatal accident.”

Nearly a thousand miles away at Delhi’s Jawaharlal Nehru University (JNU), a small set of students went on hunger strike in solidarity with students in Hyderabad. The next month a larger group attempted to march to the Education Ministry, demanding the implementation of the Rohith Vemula Act to curb caste discrimination in higher education. As campus protests spread across India (and the police retaliated with baton assaults), reports circulated that the BJP had pressured the University of Hyderabad’s authorities in the weeks leading up to Vemula’s death. (BJP ministers denied any irregular involvement in the university’s decisions.) Soon students and academics were calling for Smriti Irani, then the minister for Human Resources Development, to resign. Nothing came of that ultimatum, though Irani was “demoted” to textile minister as part of a cabinet reshuffle five months later.

During those months of unrest, a twenty-eight-year-old Muslim Ph.D. student at JNU named Umar Khalid emerged as a central figure in the broader movement. In February 2016 the Delhi police accused him and a handful of other left-leaning students of “sedition” after they organized an event marking the death anniversary of Mohammed Afzal, a Kashmiri man who had been controversially executed for a gun attack outside India’s parliament building in 2001. Hindu-nationalist sympathizers called Khalid a “Pakistani agent,” and he went into hiding. But a few days later he snuck onto JNU’s campus late at night to address a group of students, standing in front of a banner that read #JusticeForRohith.

“Friends, my name might be Umar Khalid but I am not a terrorist,” he told the crowd. Speaking into a janky microphone, he emphasized not just the injustice of his own persecution—“the way, to quote Rohith Vemula, I was reduced to my immediate identity”—but the crisis facing India’s entire higher education system. Since the BJP had come to power, students and professors had accused the government of suppressing speech on university campuses by appointing allies of the RSS in top administrative posts and making moves to overhaul syllabi. Now Khalid declared that this was “the struggle of every university in this country.” It was the responsibility of students, he insisted, to resist the corrosion of education under right-wing rule: “A university that does not teach dissent becomes a prison.” Two days later Khalid surrendered to the police. He spent nearly a month behind bars before being granted bail.

Over the years that followed, student protests would become a notable exception in a mostly cowering public sphere. In 2019, amid nationwide agitation against the Citizenship (Amendment) Act, Muslim women in Delhi led a highway-blockading sit-in, supported by students at JNU and two prominent Muslim universities, Jamia Milia Islamia and Aligarh Muslim University. Police broke into Jamia’s and AMU’s campuses and attacked students with batons and tear gas; at JNU a mob wielding iron rods and stones beat up students and teachers and vandalized buildings. Several eyewitnesses told Human Rights Watch that they identified a number of ABVP members in the mob, although none were officially held responsible and the group denied involvement. On January 27, 2020, at a rally in Delhi, a BJP minister led a chant of “shoot the traitors,” referring to Muslim protesters allied with the sit-in. Seemingly inspired by the minister’s comment, three days later a vigilante fired a pistol at protesters near Jamia’s campus.

Weeks later, another BJP minister threatened to take matters into his own hands if the police didn’t remove the protesters choking highways around the city. Groups of Hindu men gathered at various locations, and soon northeast Delhi was consumed by violence, first between the protests’ supporters and opponents, and then between Hindus and Muslims. A woman was burned alive, men were shot, and mosques, schools, and shops were set ablaze. Calm was restored only three days later, after paramilitary forces arrived at the scene. It was the worst Hindu-Muslim violence the capital had seen in decades, with fifty-three people killed, thirty-eight of them Muslim.

These riots coincided with Trump’s arrival in Delhi for his first state visit to India. While there is no evidence that Khalid, who had graduated but remained an activist, was even in Delhi back then, seven months later the Delhi police, who answer to the central government, arrested him for allegedly masterminding the violence. He was held, along with several other Muslim student activists, under the draconian Unlawful Activities (Prevention) Act of 1967, which effectively enables the government to keep people in pre-trial detention indefinitely, without bail.

Six years later, Khalid and Sharjeel Imam, another JNU history student, remain incarcerated. In a testimony published earlier this year, after the Supreme Court denied him and Imam bail, Khalid wrote that he found strength in knowing he was part of “a history that shall be penned for the future.” As a reminder, he said he had etched a quote from Bhagat Singh’s prison notebook on the wall of his cell: “Every tiny molecule of ash is in motion with my heat/I am such a Lunatic that I am free even in Jail.”

By now Khalid was seen as a dangerous revolutionary in his own right. To the authorities, the very mention of his name at the recent youth protests was threatening. In Bangalore a woman carrying a “Free Umar Khalid” poster saw it confiscated by police. Another woman at the same protest, who had held up a sign that included the phrase “Long live Umar Khalid,” was hunted down by police through CCTV surveillance footage; she was later slapped with an incident report, with an investigation underway. When, according to reporting from The Indian Express, some protesters were said to have brought “Free Umar Khalid” posters to a solidarity demonstration in Goa, the local police detained at least two people and grilled them about whether they knew of Khalid’s “background” and if they had shouted slogans in his support (and if so, how many times). Among the two hundred and forty points in the questionnaire the police gave them was the question: “What is your understanding of the words ‘Free Umar Khalid?’”

But Khalid had also become a vexed symbol for the protesters themselves. When a BJP minister tried to malign the protests by dredging up a CJP spokesperson’s old tweets in support of Khalid, the CJP leader in question seemed to sidestep expressing a view on Khalid’s imprisonment, saying only that the group was focused on educational reform. This hesitance disappointed the CJP’s allies on the left, who argued that Khalid’s story was part of the same student struggle. Several weeks later, Neha Bora, the AISA leader who went on hunger strike, declared: “Umar Khalid is not a question of nationalist or anti-national…. It is a question of what kind of country we want to build.”

Some protesters tried to censor mentions of Khalid among the crowd for fear of government retribution, pleading with fellow demonstrators to put away their FREE UMAR KHALID signs. Yet I saw others at the actions brandish copies of Fractured Communities, Khalid’s recently published Ph.D. dissertation on the history of eastern Indian indigenous groups under British rule. One protester also held up a handwritten poster, an intimation of the significance of Khalid’s thinking and organizing, that gained particular approval on social media: “UMAR KHALID walked so Gen Z could run.”

Now that they, too, found themselves labelled “anti-national terrorists,” perhaps this segment of young protesters were coming to understand what Khalid had long preached. In his view an authoritarian government can only be fought if students build bridges between their struggles and those of Muslims, Dalits, laborers, indigenous communities, and peasants—if, that is, they fight Hindu nationalism head-on. Although the mainstream of the recent student protests has tried hard to avoid this kind of direct attack, in the protests’ aftermath the state’s own behavior is forcing them to drop the façade that their actions have no ideological dimension: Muslim volunteers have faced detentions and vigilante violence, and in his Independence Day speech Modi equated dissidents with Maoist separatists, calling them “intellectual naxals.” By early August Dipke, the CJP’s founder, was pressed to admit that Khalid deserved a fair trial.

Four days after the state ruthlessly cracked down at Jantar Mantar, the movement seemed desperate for some kind of payoff. A few hundred meters away from the center of the protest site, on the road toward parliament, I observed hundreds of demonstrators facing down police and paramilitary troops. A chain of harried volunteers tried to keep sections of the crowd from escalating the confrontation. Then, unexpectedly, past midnight, Wangchuk broke his fast. Sharing a photo of BJP officials surrounding his hospital bed, he said they had promised to address the protesters’ concerns in parliament. Less than an hour earlier Modi had appeared in a selfie-style Instagram video, vowing to pass an education reform bill.

The CJP’s leaders expressed relief at the prospect of Wangchuk’s recovery but distanced themselves from his decision to make peace with BJP ministers, keeping the protest going without him. Online, meanwhile, neither Modi’s tacky video nor—as one social media user put it—its late-night “fuckboy” timing went over well with its intended Gen Z audience; a barrage of reels mocked his nostril-focused camerawork, drawling tone, and labored attempts to sound cool by addressing protesters as “friends.”

The following day police fired several rounds of tear gas on Parliament Street. Some protesters toppled barricades; earlier I had seen people perched on trees, hurling empty water bottles and sticks at the officers, and now a larger number launched similar objects from the ground. The police in turn beat the demonstrators they could grab from the fast-receding crowd. Minutes later, Pradhan, the education minister, announced his resignation on X. (Conspicuously, he didn’t admit to any wrongdoing.)

As the news spread through the crowd, people shrieked and jumped. Cries of “We won!” and “Long live the revolution!” rang out. A few hours later the CJP, saying that the government had assured them it wouldn’t penalize protesters in the coming days, called the protest to an end. For most of the demonstrators it was a day of victory, although others worried that the protests had been called off prematurely, just when the movement had gathered steam. While celebrating with their friends, some students told me they wondered what else they could have demanded had they kept going.

In the following days, skepticism over the government’s olive branch would prove to be justified. Overnight, as the police cleared the protest site of people and paraphernalia, the government started reneging on its promise not to retaliate. More than a hundred protesters across the country found themselves facing criminal charges; The Indian Express reported that the Delhi police, scavenging through piles of garbage at Jantar Mantar for labeled packaging, targeted restaurants in the city that had supplied food to protesters. Attempting to salvage the situation, the CJP threatened to reestablish the encampment. The government then scrambled to assure the CJP it would hold up its end of the bargain—although more than a month later it has refused to provide the Supreme Court with a list of incident reports against protesters so the court can dismiss those cases.

The Modi regime seems to be waiting for the discontent to blow over. Opposition leaders have been calling for parliamentary debate about the protests, but the government has refused to come to the table. Pradhan has been replaced by another, arguably still more Hindu-supremacist education minister, Pralhad Joshi, who also has fewer educational qualifications than his predecessor. (In 2022 Joshi defended the premature release of eleven Hindu men convicted of raping a Muslim woman.) Delhi police, meanwhile, have directed social media platforms to remove any content with what one report calls “offensive remarks” against the prime minister.

On July 31 Modi released another selfie video “forgiving” the “naughty children” who had used abusive language against him, but an army of online trolls—which in another instance The Washington Post has directly linked to the BJP’s IT infrastructure—continued to bombard women protesters with rape and death threats. A fifteen-year-old girl who called the prime minister a “dick” was forced to issue a public apology because of a hate campaign that has by now forced her and her family to move.

The movement, however, seems to be pushing on. In the past months it has, on the whole, left the capital for the inner reaches of the country. In the eastern state of Jharkhand, college students went on hunger strike to protest irregularities in a state employment exam. Delegations from both AISA and the CJP traveled to Jharkhand in support before embarking on separate nationwide advocacy tours. After nearly a month of protesting, the Jharkhand students suspended their agitation when the state government, which is not allied with the BJP, conceded to some of their demands. More recently in August, police in the BJP-ruled state of Bihar fired water canons at protesters marching to the chief minister’s house to insist that the state administer its recruitment exams more fairly. A panel of students, part of the wider education-related protests in Bihar, later agreed to call off the agitation after the government acquiesced to a major demand.

The most surprising development is the movement’s broadening constituency. Schoolchildren in various parts of India have been striking for more teaching staff and better facilities, a trend that social media users have described as “Gen Alpha rising.” The CJP, which has chosen to remain a pressure group rather than enter electoral politics, has now adopted primary education as its next big cause.

The movement’s diffuse quality is both its strength and its greatest challenge. While it’s senseless to expect any mass protest to be doctrinaire, it would also be foolish to try to separate out the BJP’s administrative failures from its clear ideological project. If the movement wants to keep up the pressure and eventually force some kind of consequential electoral change, it will in all likelihood have to marry its ecumenical demands with a more explicit indictment of the BJP’s unrelenting schismatic politics.

Generations of the country’s student protesters have stressed precisely this point. Six years into his imprisonment, Umar Khalid composed a public letter to Rohith Vemula: “Dear Rohith, On a cold starry night, I look at the sky from my prison cell. I spot the brightest star and imagine it’s you smiling at me from up there.” Khalid wished that Vemula was with him in freedom, so they could not just compare their “frustrations” and “romances” but “debate and decipher what went wrong in the life of this Republic.” It was clear to him that this sort of political consciousness among students was what the government was so desperate to preempt. “By pushing you to death and by putting me in prison, they ensured that this conversation could never materialise,” he wrote. “Because this is what the regime fears—young thinking people.”

entries.title: ‘You’ll Never Catch Him!’
entries.summary: Paul Julian just wanted everyone to get out of the way.
